Lattice
LAT-iss
noun
From Old French lattis, from latte, a lath — a network of crossed laths or bars forming a screen over a window. It renders Hebrew eshnab (H822) and charak (H2762), the pierced or netted window-screen of an eastern house.

Biblical Definition

The lattice is the crossed screen of laths or bars set over an eastern window, through which one looked out or was glimpsed within, half-seen and half-hid. Scripture uses it in three scenes of watching and being watched. First, the mother of Sisera “looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming?” (Jdg 5:28) — a heathen mother straining through the screen for a son who lay slain, a picture of vain hope peering after what will never return. Second, King Ahaziah “fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber” (2Ki 1:2) and, seeking Baalzebub rather than the LORD, died for it — the frail screen giving way, and the idolater falling through the very thing he leaned upon. But the third use lifts the word to glory: in the Song, the Bride says of her Beloved, “he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice” (Son 2:9). Here Christ is figured as One who, before the full unveiling, shews Himself through the lattice — giving His Church partial, tender, real glimpses of His face through the screen of ordinances, of Scripture, of providence, until the day the wall is taken down and we see Him face to face. The same crossed screen that framed a heathen mother’s vain watching and an idol-king’s deadly fall becomes, in the mouth of the Bride, the very lattice through which the Bridegroom lets His beloved catch sight of Him. What we now see through the lattice, we shall then see without a veil.

Webster 1828 Definition

A window-screen of crossed laths or bars; the eastern lattice through which one looked out or was glimpsed within.

expand to see more

LATTICE, noun. Any work of wood or metal made by crossing laths, rods, or bars, and forming open squares or lozenges between them.

A window or screen so made, admitting air and sight while veiling the interior.

In Scripture, the screen through which Sisera’s mother cried, watching for her son (Jdg 5:28).

The frail lattice through which Ahaziah fell to his death in Samaria (2Ki 1:2).

The lattice through which the Beloved sheweth Himself to His Bride (Son 2:9).

Key Scripture

Jdg 5:28 — "The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?"

2Ki 1:2 — "And Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease."

Son 2:9 — "My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice."

2Co 3:18 — "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord."

Modern Corruption

A window-screen of the eastern house, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the sweet truth that Christ now shews Himself in part, until the veil is taken away.

expand to see more

The temptation the lattice rebukes is the twin error of despising the partial and demanding the total — either scorning the real glimpses of Christ granted through Word and ordinance because they are not yet the full vision, or, like Sisera’s mother, straining through the lattice after a false hope that will never come. Ahaziah leaned upon a frail screen and an idol and fell through both. The lattice teaches us to prize the true sight given now and to lean on the right object.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Bridegroom shews Himself through the lattice — that the Church’s present knowledge of Christ, though partial, is real and precious: we see now through a glass darkly, but then face to face (1Co 13:12). What is glimpsed through the screen of ordinances shall one day be beheld without a veil, when the wall is taken down and faith gives way to sight.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew eshnab (H822) and charak (H2762), the netted or pierced window-screen of an eastern house.

expand to see more

Hebrew eshnab (H822) — a latticed window or casement (Jdg 5:28; Pro 7:6)

Hebrew charak (H2762) — a lattice or window-screen (Son 2:9)

Old French lattis, from latte, a lath — crossed laths forming an open screen

A place of watching (Sisera’s mother), of falling (Ahaziah), and of gracious glimpsing (the Beloved)

Figures the partial sight of Christ now, answering to “through a glass, darkly” (1Co 13:12)

Usage

"The Beloved sheweth Himself through the lattice, granting His Bride true if partial sight of His face."

"Sisera’s mother cried through the lattice for a son who would never come — the peering of vain hope."

"What the Church now sees through the lattice she shall one day behold face to face."
